title: Precept Eight - Non-Being Stingy
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The talk's main teaching invites listeners to explore the concept of "non-being stingy" by recognizing how we often hold onto things we perceive as lacking or scarce, such as tension, contraction, or scarcity of resources. By softening our hearts and embracing openness, we can cultivate a sense of generosity and receive freely, letting go of ignorance and interdependence. This practice is rooted in the precept of generosity, which encourages us to turn away from isolation and self-restriction, and instead embody kindness and relatedness in every moment.

sentences.text: Oh, non-being stingy.
This is another one I can relate to.
Nancy Baker uses the word tight to describe what it feels like to be stingy—tight.
That really spoke to me.
I'm a body worker, so I'm going to invite you to do a little exercise with me to exaggerate the tension patterns in your body.
Hold yourself tight.
Contract your muscles, squeeze your eyes closed, pull your arms close to the midline, make a fist, bring your knees together, squeeze yourself tight, and just notice how that feels.
And then, while you're holding yourself tight, try to reach out, try to reach a hand out to touch, to make an offering.
It's hard, isn't it?
When you're holding yourself tight, you can relax for a minute.
But this is one way we give, right?
We make offerings through the deeds that our hands perform in the world; we make offerings by giving gifts.

But if we're holding ourselves tight, and we all have holding patterns—there isn't a single one of us that doesn't have a holding pattern in our body, how we hold our posture, our gait, our movement—so we're all constricted in some way.
So humor me one more time.
Hold yourself tight, squeeze in, squeeze your mouth closed, squeeze your eyes closed.
Now imagine, from this tight place, softening your heart.
It's hard; I feel myself close up around the heart.
That's what my body does.
But of course, it's from the heart that we make offerings from this wellspring of compassion.
It's through touch, maybe offering a hug to someone we love, maybe offering caring touch to someone in pain, maybe offering a sandwich to a homeless person on the street.
I invite you one more time for another experiment: to hold yourself tight, contract all your muscles, pull all your energy in.
Now try to take a deep breath.
Oh my goodness, again, constriction.
And if we can't receive the breath, if we can't receive, how can we give?
It's a two-way street, a reciprocal relationship.
When we exhale, we offer carbon dioxide to the trees, but only after we inhale to receive the oxygen that nurtures ourselves.
There's a continual give and take when we open, when we soften.
How was that for you guys?
Before I go on, I relate to things a little bit through body workers' eyes.
There are many ways of being stingy.
It took me about a minute to rattle off a list here of all the ways that I can see stinginess in myself.
Sometimes we are stingy with money, out of fear of not having enough, or possibly out of greed for wanting more.
Wanting.
Wanting.
We might be stingy with our heart, maybe because we've been hurt, maybe our heart has been broken, betrayed, so we hold back our heart.
Maybe we're stingy with time, right?
That's an interesting one.
I'm stingy with my time, especially when I'm hooked by the feeling that there's not enough.
And I ask myself, how can that be?
Time is eternal.
How could there not be enough?
But I'm caught by these constructs of time that we live by.
Maybe we're stingy about sharing ourselves, holding back our feelings, our gifts, our insights, our needs, or who we really are.
This is something to think about: how do you hold yourself back?
And how about being stingy with giving yourself over to this moment one hundred percent wholeheartedly?
Just this right here, right now.
What's in front of you?
Nancy Baker says in her chapter on non-stinginess, we're stingy with anything we hold on to, with anything going on for us, that we are unwilling to open to.
We're stingy when we're not fully participating in what's happening right here, right now.
It seems so simple, but it's not, because we have our preferences.

And of course, that's at the heart of our practice: to notice these preferences and bring ourselves back right here, right now, regardless of whether it's the way we want it to be or not, the way we like it to be or not.
Here's another question: are you stingy with gratitude?
Like really appreciating the cashier who offered you a smile with the correct change at the grocery store today?
Or appreciating the hardworking farmers that harvested your food?
I come from California in the Central Valley where it's so hot, harvesting in the heat, so you could have freshly ripened vegetables or fruit.
Or appreciating the mail person, so coming back to Washington, who trudges around your neighborhood in the rain to deliver your mail, so on and so forth.
The list could be endless.
There are infinitude—is that a word?—infinite things to be grateful for.
And you know what?
Sometimes, regardless of that, I find myself complaining.
Are you stingy with receiving as well as giving?
Think about this one: are you able to receive compliments?
Are you able to receive credit for what you did or who you are?
I sometimes find myself minimizing these compliments; I'm shying away from being seen.
And then Nancy Baker points out that any bargaining, manipulating, negotiating are all expressions of stinginess.
In other words, we give to get; it's like a tit for tat.
And sometimes this is very subtle and often unconscious.
For example, we might give a compliment when actually we want to receive one, or we may give attention in order to get attention.
We might make an offering, a generous offering, maybe to be seen as a giving person.
Sometimes I'm stingy about expressing my needs because I don't want to be seen as a needy person or as burdensome.

I found it really interesting when I looked at Diane Risotto's book on the precepts that she merged the two precepts in her wording: "I take up the way of taking only what is freely given, so not taking what's not mine, and giving freely all that I can."
I take up the way of taking only what is freely given and giving freely all that I can.
So non-greed and non-being stingy, right, are like two sides of the same coin.
Taking is on one side of the coin while giving is on the other.
As if there's a distinction, but really, it's like the inhale and the exhale, one breath.
She quotes Henry Miller who says, *the universe is engaged in a reciprocal dance of give and take.
We can't have one without the other.

Of course, you can't have an inhale without an exhale or vice versa.* So I noticed when I feel into the practice of non-greed and non-stinginess that they both arise for me out of a feeling of lack or a belief in lack.
I take what's not mine or I hold on to what I have when I believe that there's not enough, that I don't have enough, that I'm not enough.
Maybe I'm not good enough.
There's lack on some level, whether it be material, emotional or spiritual, and that makes me want and it makes me hold on.
So here's where I meet face to face again my separate sense of self, my belief in what Okumura calls the limited individual self.
It's only the limited individual self that sees through this lens of not enough.
In reality, each person is Buddha, complete, perfect, and life gives endlessly.

I've been rereading Norman Fischer's book on the Paramitas, *The World Could Be Otherwise*, and in his chapter on the Paramita of Generosity, he says to practice it, generosity, is to appreciate the natural abundance of being, the inherent generosity of time and space and the ongoing unfoldment of life.
These are generous gifts.
Life itself is generous.
Life is always making more.
Life is abundant and expansive, not stingy or small-minded.
It keeps on going, bubbling up and expanding wherever it has a chance.
It's so true.
We've paved over so much of the earth with roads and sidewalks, and there's one crack in the sidewalk and life emerges from it.
It's kind of miraculous.
Life can't stop giving itself.
So practicing with non-being stingy reminds me that in reality, there's nothing lacking.
At the same time, practicing with this precept highlights my habit patterns of holding on, of not giving freely.
But over time, practicing with the precepts allows each of us to open that, to open to all that life is giving.
Reb Anderson refers to this precept as non-being possessive, not being possessive—excuse me.
Nancy Baker uses the language of non-very intentionally.
But Reb uses more traditional language, not being possessive.
He says this precept points to a disease and wonder.
The disease is stinginess.
The wonder is giving.
Stinginess is a tightness; there's that word again.
Tightness, a constriction of the heart.
It is born of ignorance, ignorance of interdependence, not realizing how our lives are embraced and sustained by the kindness of all beings.
Stinginess is turning away from the relatedness toward isolation.
And as we turn away from others, we also turn away from ourselves.
So again, this precept points us to the first paramita, the paramita of generosity, giving freely.
This paramita, the first paramita includes all the others of prime importance.
I believe it points to the heart of this practice, which is not about sitting down, as much about standing up.
It's not about how calm and equanimous or equanimous you are on your meditation cushion.
It's about how kind and generous you are when you get up off the cushion.
And that's the heart of the Bodhisattva path: to benefit others, to give freely, to help, to support, to share your heart of compassion.
I'm very aware tonight, with the exception of Saturday morning, it concludes this shared exploration we've been on of each of the precepts.
So I want to finish by circling back to the title of the book that we chose for our text, *Opening to Oneness*.
We've talked a lot about different ways to practice with these precepts, but not so explicitly about the three levels of practice that are often referred to when working with the precepts.
The first level is the literal, the second is the relative, and the third is the level of the absolute.

And the literal level is just as it sounds, literal: never pull a weed from your garden, never swat at a mosquito, never form, let alone articulate, a harsh or hurtful thought, not even about politicians that you don't like, never hold back the truth.
That's a horizon we'll never reach.
The relative level of practice takes into account the conditioned nature of perception.
For example, I might be given an invitation to lunch by a friend and need to say no thank you.
And one person might feel actually hurt or rejected by my decline.
Another person could be just fine with it.
So while we may aim never to hurt another person, it's actually impossible because no matter what we do, there'll be somebody that's triggered by our actions or our speech.
They see through their own lens of conditioning.
And we may choose, we may believe that we're choosing kind words, "no thank you," but they may hear it because of the lenses that they wear quite differently.
The relative level also takes into account the complexity of our relationships and the complexity of the relationships between the precepts.
In other words, I could be a guest at your house and you could serve me eggplant.
I don't like eggplant that much.

So, you know, am I just going to smile and say, "thank you so much, this is lovely," somebody made a great effort to make me eggplant parmesan, or am I going to say, "yuck, is there something else I can eat here?"
So it's not always appropriate to say the most honest thing.
When Hitler's Nazi soldiers knock on your door in search of a Jew that you're hiding, is it better to save that person's life or tell the truth?
So as you can see, there isn't a correct way to practice with the precepts; they're relative to circumstances.
Practicing on the level of the absolute really means no longer practicing the precepts—the precepts practice themselves.
Like Suzuki Roshi says, when we function from an embodied knowing of oneness, the precepts naturally arise from our true nature.
There's no effort.
We simply open to what is.
It may sound like these three levels are like a step ladder moving from a more rudimentary or grosser level, practicing with the precepts, to a more refined or advanced level.
But it's not like that.
It's not a linear process.
We're continually moving between the three levels, right?
We remember who we are and we forget who we are.
We open to oneness and we close to oneness.
We have deep-seated, conditioned beliefs about our separate sense of self.
They come and at times take a strong hold on our consciousness.
And at other times, the grip on our consciousness loosens.
So while I may, and I actually do feel a strong pull to know my true nature, I also feel a strong pull to reinforce what I've been conditioned to believe about myself.
So I need to practice the precepts on every level.
And sometimes I need to let the practice go.
The precepts happen just like the breath happens opening to oneness.
So we're going to head into breakout rooms.
Maybe Tim has created breakout rooms.
Do you want to put the questions in the chat box, Tim, or shall I go ahead and do that?
I can do that.
Okay.
So there's two repeating questions.
Alternate the two questions for five minutes.
No, ten minutes, excuse me.
Alternate the two questions for ten minutes, asking your partner and then you switch and you alternate the two questions for ten minutes in the reverse direction.
The questions are: "Tell me your way you're stingy."
Thank you.
"What do you believe is lacking?"
Thank you.
"Tell me your way you're stingy."
And you know what?
You could say, "I don't know."
You could say, "I don't have anything to say to you right now."
And as the questioner, you just say thank you and continue.
We'll see what happens.
Should I fire them up?
I'm ready.
Does everybody feel ready?
